questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The four subject matters of a lobbying contact
questions.learningObjective: Identify which four subject matters define a lobbying contact
questions.stem: Under the lobbying disclosure statute, a lobbying contact concerns which of the following sets of subject matters?

options.text: Only legislation and nominations pending before Congress
options.misconception: narrows the scope to two matters and omits rules and programs

options.text: Legislation, treaties, executive orders, and judicial appointments
options.misconception: substitutes matters drawn from other constitutional sources

options.text: Any communication with a covered official regardless of subject matter
options.misconception: ignores the statutory subject-matter filter entirely

questions.explanation: The statute defines a lobbying contact by four subject matters: legislation, rules, programs, and nominations. Option A omits rules and programs, while C and D misstate the scope.
questions.hint: Recall the four statutory subject matters that trigger disclosure.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Who the statute counts as a lobbyist
questions.learningObjective: Define who qualifies as a lobbyist under the disclosure act
questions.stem: A person qualifies as a lobbyist only if they satisfy which two conditions?

options.text: They make a lobbying contact and are employed or retained for compensation
They make a lobbying contact and receive income or spend over the threshold
options.misconception: states only one of the two required conditions

options.text: They are retained by a foreign principal and file a registration
options.misconception: confuses the statute with foreign-agent registration

options.text: They communicate with any federal employee on any topic
options.misconception: drops both the contact and compensation requirements

questions.explanation: A lobbyist must both make a lobbying contact and be employed or retained for compensation. B states only one condition, while A and D misstate the test.
questions.hint: Both a contact and compensation are required.

options.text: They are excluded unless they are billed to a client
options.misconception: adds a billing condition the statute does not require

options.text: They count as part of the lobbying activity itself

options.misconception: assumes volunteer status removes the activity from scope

options.text: They must be reported only if they exceed twenty hours

questions.explanation: Preparatory and supporting efforts are treated as part of the lobbying activity. The other options add conditions the statute does not impose.
questions.hint: Support work is folded into the lobbying activity.

questions.topic: The income figure that exempts a registrant
questions.learningObjective: State the income threshold that exempts a registrant
questions.stem: A registrant is exempt when total income from lobbying activities does not exceed what dollar amount?
questions.explanation: The statute exempts a registrant whose total income from lobbying activities does not exceed five thousand dollars. This small threshold keeps minor activity out of the system.
questions.hint: The exemption floor is five thousand dollars.

questions.explanation: Registration is due within forty-five days after the first lobbying contact. This window gives firms time to file without delaying transparency.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The honest-broker account of organised interests
questions.learningObjective: Describe the honest-broker view of organised interests
questions.stem: Explain the honest-broker account of how organised interests operate in policy making.

answer.exemplar: The honest-broker account holds that organised interests supply information and expertise to policymakers, acting as neutral intermediaries that improve decision quality rather than skew it toward private gain.

questions.explanation: The honest-broker view casts groups as information providers, not as buyers of policy. It assumes competition among groups keeps any single interest from dominating.
questions.hint: Groups act as neutral information providers.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The collective-action problem in group formation
questions.learningObjective: Explain the collective-action problem in group formation
questions.stem: Why do large groups often fail to form even when their members share a common interest?

answer.exemplar: Large groups struggle because benefits are shared by all while costs fall on individuals, so each member free-rides and no one organises, a classic collective-action problem.

questions.explanation: Shared benefits and private costs create free-riding, which blocks organisation unless selective incentives are offered. This is the core collective-action dilemma.
questions.hint: Shared benefits with private costs invite free-riding.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Applying the statutory definition of lobbyist
questions.learningObjective: Apply the statutory definition of lobbyist
questions.stem: A consultant who makes one lobbying contact and is paid ten thousand dollars for it is what?

options.text: Not a lobbyist because the payment is a flat fee
options.misconception: assumes fee structure matters to the definition

options.text: A lobbyist only if registered with the state
options.misconception: adds a state-registration condition

options.text: Exempt because only one contact was made
options.misconception: assumes a minimum number of contacts

options.text: A lobbyist under the statutory definition

questions.explanation: One contact plus compensation satisfies the definition. The other options add conditions the statute does not require.
questions.hint: One contact with compensation suffices.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The default rule and the route to stopping a rule
questions.learningObjective: State the default rule and how to stop a rule
questions.stem: Under congressional review, what is the default for a submitted rule?

options.text: The rule takes effect unless Congress disapproves it
The rule is blocked until Congress affirmatively approves it
options.misconception: reverses the default to require approval

options.text: The rule expires after thirty days automatically
options.misconception: invents an automatic expiration

options.text: The rule is sent to the President for signature
options.misconception: confuses rulemaking with legislation

questions.explanation: The default is that the rule takes effect unless disapproved. The other options reverse or misstate the default.
questions.hint: Default is effect unless disapproved.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The four subject matters of a lobbying contact
questions.learningObjective: Apply the four subject matters to a scenario
questions.stem: A meeting to discuss a pending agency rule concerns which subject matter?

options.text: Legislation
options.misconception: confuses a rule with a bill

options.text: Nominations
options.misconception: confuses rulemaking with appointments

options.text: Rules
Programs
options.misconception: confuses a rule with a program

questions.explanation: A pending agency rule falls under the rules subject matter. The other options misclassify it.
questions.hint: A pending rule is the rules matter.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Who the statute counts as a lobbyist
questions.learningObjective: Apply the lobbyist definition to a volunteer
questions.stem: A volunteer who lobbies without pay and makes lobbying contacts is a lobbyist?

options.text: Yes, because contacts alone suffice
options.misconception: drops the compensation requirement

options.text: No, because volunteers are exempt by category
options.misconception: assumes a categorical volunteer exemption

options.text: Yes, if the contacts exceed three
options.misconception: invents a contact-count threshold

options.text: No, because compensation is required

questions.explanation: Compensation is required, so an unpaid volunteer is not a lobbyist. The other options misstate the test.
questions.hint: No compensation means not a lobbyist.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The efforts that support a lobbying contact
questions.learningObjective: Apply the supporting-efforts rule
questions.stem: Time spent researching a bill before a meeting with a senator counts as what?

options.text: Part of the lobbying activity
Unreportable preparation
options.misconception: assumes preparation is excluded

options.text: A separate consulting service
options.misconception: splits preparation from lobbying

options.text: Overhead not attributable to any client
options.misconception: treats preparation as general overhead

questions.explanation: Preparatory research counts as part of the lobbying activity. The other options wrongly exclude it.
questions.hint: Preparation is folded into lobbying.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The income figure that exempts a registrant
questions.learningObjective: Apply the income exemption threshold
questions.stem: A firm earned four thousand dollars from lobbying; how much more can it earn and stay exempt?
questions.explanation: The exemption floor is five thousand dollars, so four thousand leaves one thousand dollars of room. The arithmetic is five thousand minus four thousand.
questions.hint: Subtract four thousand from five thousand.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: When a registrant must register
questions.learningObjective: Compute a registration deadline date
questions.stem: If the first lobbying contact occurs on day 10 of the year, by what day must registration be filed?
questions.explanation: Registration is due within forty-five days after the first contact, so day ten plus forty-five equals day fifty-five.
questions.hint: Add forty-five days to day ten.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The honest-broker account of organised interests
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the honest-broker account
questions.stem: A critic of the honest-broker account would most likely say what?

options.text: Groups never provide any information to policymakers
options.misconception: overstates the critique to an absurd extreme

options.text: Groups are always regulated by the courts
options.misconception: introduces judicial oversight not in the debate

options.text: Groups skew information to favor their own interests
Groups cannot influence legislation at all
options.misconception: denies influence that the account concedes

questions.explanation: Critics argue groups skew information for self-interest. The other options overstate or misstate the critique.
questions.hint: Critics point to biased information.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The collective-action problem in group formation
questions.learningObjective: Apply the collective-action problem
questions.stem: A large consumer group struggles to form because each consumer what?

options.text: Prefers to lobby alone for greater gain
options.misconception: assumes strategic solo lobbying

options.text: Lacks any shared interest in prices
options.misconception: denies the common interest that creates the problem

options.text: Is legally barred from joining
options.misconception: invents a legal barrier

options.text: Benefits only if others pay the costs

questions.explanation: Each consumer benefits regardless of paying, so free-riding blocks formation. The other options misstate the barrier.
questions.hint: Free-riding blocks large-group formation.

questions.topic: Clienteliage and the exchange of help for loyalty
questions.learningObjective: Apply clienteliage to a scenario
questions.stem: A politician who provides jobs to supporters in exchange for votes illustrates what?

options.text: Pluralist competition
options.misconception: confuses clienteliage with pluralism

options.text: Merit-based hiring
options.misconception: confuses patronage with merit

options.text: Clienteliage
Iron law of oligarchy
options.misconception: confuses exchange with leadership drift

questions.explanation: Jobs for votes is a clientelistic exchange. The other options misclassify the relationship.
questions.hint: Help for loyalty is clienteliage.

questions.topic: The pluralism and elitist disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Apply the pluralism-elitism debate
questions.stem: A researcher who finds that a few wealthy donors dominate policy outcomes supports which view?

options.text: Pluralism
options.misconception: confuses concentration with dispersion

options.text: Rational choice
options.misconception: confuses power concentration with individual calculus

options.text: Institutionalism
options.misconception: confuses donor power with institutional rules

options.text: Elitism

questions.explanation: Concentrated donor power supports elitism. The other options misclassify the finding.
questions.hint: Concentrated power supports elitism.

options.text: The iron law of oligarchy
Pluralist competition
options.misconception: confuses leadership drift with competition

options.text: Clienteliage
options.misconception: confuses oligarchy with patronage

options.text: Collective action
options.misconception: confuses leadership drift with group formation

questions.explanation: Unaccountable officers illustrate oligarchic drift. The other options misclassify the pattern.
questions.hint: Leadership drift is the iron law.

options.text: A pluralist coalition
options.misconception: confuses the triangle with broad competition

options.text: An iron triangle
A clientelistic exchange
options.misconception: confuses institutional ties with patronage

questions.explanation: The three actors form an iron triangle. The other options misclassify the arrangement.
questions.hint: Agency, committee, industry form the triangle.

options.text: A clientelistic exchange

options.text: A merit system
options.misconception: confuses policy debate with personnel rules

options.text: An issue network

Elitism

options.text: Pluralism

options.text: Behavioralism

options.text: Excepted service

options.text: Merit principles

questions.topic: Why career staff are protected from partisan removal

Greater expertise in agencies

options.text: Lower compliance costs for small firms
options.misconception: confuses staffing with regulatory burden

options.text: Faster congressional confirmation

options.text: The competitive service exam
options.misconception: confuses exams with retaliation protection

options.text: Whistleblower reprisal protection
The lobbying disclosure act
options.misconception: confuses lobbying with personnel protection

options.text: The duty to register lobbyists

options.text: The duty to consult Congress
options.misconception: confuses review with consultation

options.text: The duty of continuing review

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A rule that passes the review window
questions.learningObjective: Apply the review-window outcome
questions.stem: A rule submitted sixty days ago with no congressional action now what?

options.text: It is void for lack of approval
options.misconception: reverses the default

options.text: It must be resubmitted
options.misconception: assumes inaction requires resubmission

options.text: It takes effect
It is held in abeyance
options.misconception: treats silence as a hold

questions.explanation: With no disapproval, the rule takes effect. The other options misstate the outcome.
questions.hint: No action means the rule proceeds.

questions.stem: After Congress disapproves a rule, the agency may reissue it only if what?

options.text: It waits thirty days and refiles the same text
options.misconception: assumes a cooling-off period suffices

options.text: The committee chair consents in writing
options.misconception: adds a committee consent condition

options.text: The President directs reissuance by memo
options.misconception: adds a presidential directive condition

options.text: The new rule is not substantially the same

questions.explanation: Reissuance requires a rule not substantially the same. The other options add unsupported conditions.
questions.hint: The reissued rule must differ in substance.
